description:
Hi! I'm based in Mexico City and interested in data analysis, data science, and software development. I work with Python, data processing, and visualization, and use AI-assisted tools to build software.

For Space Apps, I'm designing GAIA, a web platform to explore environmental trends using NASA data and statistical analysis. I'll contribute to requirements, data analysis, and implementation.

I value teamwork, curiosity, and building something useful and scientifically sound.
summary:
GAIA is a web prototype for investigating how rainfall changes across regions and seasons. It addresses NASA Space Apps’ “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” challenge by asking whether annual precipitation totals can hide changes in specific months or seasons.

The prototype is designed to let users select a time period and compare two regions using an interactive map and time-series charts. For each region, GAIA estimates how much precipitation changes per decade and shows the uncertainty and statistical evidence behind that estimate. It also flags when too few observations are available to draw a conclusion.

This matters because two regions can have similar annual rainfall totals while experiencing different changes in when rain falls. Looking at seasonal and annual results together helps users see where those changes occur and judge how confidently they can interpret them.
details:
What GAIA does

GAIA (Geospatial Analysis for Investigating Anomalies) is a web prototype for exploring regional rainfall trends. It investigates a question inspired by NASA Space Apps’ “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” challenge: can annual rainfall totals hide meaningful changes in individual months or seasons?

How it works

The prototype is designed around an interactive map and time-series charts. Users select a period and a month or season, then inspect results for two predefined regions alongside their annual totals. GAIA’s analysis estimates the rate of change in millimeters per decade using the Theil–Sen estimator, reports a 95% confidence interval, and uses a two-sided Mann–Kendall test to assess statistical significance. A series needs at least 20 valid years and 80% coverage for GAIA to report a trend. The analysis retains gaps and treats a season as incomplete if any required month is missing.

What makes it creative and useful

GAIA makes the annual total part of the investigation. A wetter season and a drier season can offset each other in the annual sum. By examining both scales, users can see where those changes occur, measure their size, and judge how much evidence supports them. The intended impact is to make Earth science data easier to investigate and help users communicate a defensible finding, including when the available evidence is inconclusive.

Tools and design considerations

The MVP uses React, TypeScript, React Router, and Vite for the web interface, MapLibre GL JS for the map, and Recharts for the time series. The backend uses Python and FastAPI, with a fixed set of monthly observations stored in read-only SQLite. The application is designed to run locally on a standard computer, without accounts, and to serve its map resources offline once installed.

I prioritized comparable time periods, clear units, traceable data sources, and explicit handling of missing observations. We limited the first version to two regions so the team could focus on verifying the calculations and making the results easy to interpret.
